description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes how the Augustenborg neighbourhood of Malmö, Sweden, which flooded every year in the late 1990s because its combined drainage could not cope with runoff and household waste water, was regenerated between 1998 and 2002 as the Ekostaden (Eco-city) Augustenborg project. Sustainable urban drainage was retrofitted around existing buildings and utilities: about 6 km of canals and water channels, ten retention ponds, green roofs including a botanical roof garden, and ditches that pass surplus water to the conventional sewer, designed for a 15-year rainfall event. The work was led by the MKB housing company and the City of Malmö with residents, cost about SEK 200 million (around 24 million euros) with national LIP and EU LIFE funding, and has been operational since May 2001. The page, first published in 2017 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal with a brochure and links. Caveats: no climate change analysis was done for the system, space had to be found around electricity, water, heating and telephone networks, and some residents lost usable green space. It illustrates climate adaptation of urban drainage through green and blue infrastructure and flood hazard reduction; related records are the Copenhagen Cloudburst Management Plan case study and the Copernicus Urban Atlas.
name: Urban stormwater management in Augustenborg, Malmö (Ekostaden Augustenborg)
outcomes: Annual flooding stopped after the open stormwater system of 6 km of channels and ten ponds became operational in 2001, and the area's image and environment improved.
